description: We are Developers, a team passionate about Artificial Intelligence, coding, and space science. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to build FlameGuard AI, an intelligent platform that analyzes NASA's microgravity combustion experiments and provides useful fire safety insights for future space missions. We welcome AI/ML developers, Python programmers, data analysts, web developers, UI/UX designers, and space science enthusiasts. Beginners are welcome too!
summary: Flame in Freefall is an interactive, SI-assisted dashboard that turns NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion research into accessible fire-safety insight. It organizes 14 PSI investigations—BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, FLEX-2, SAFFIRE I–III, SAME, SAME-R, ACME BRE, ACME CFI-G, SLICE, SPICE, and CFI—into a searchable experiment explorer, a side-by-side comparison tool, an evidence library, and charts for oxygen, pressure, airflow, flame spread, suppression, and smoke. Every value carries a provenance label: NASA-measured, published finding, AI interpretation, or illustrative demonstration data. The Ask Science Copilot retrieves relevant records and, when configured, uses Gemini to produce a constrained answer; otherwise it returns a deterministic local fallback with citations. The project matters because Moon and Mars habitats may use oxygen-enriched, low-pressure atmospheres where fire behaves differently than on Earth. It helps students, engineers, and mission planners explore the evidence, compare test conditions, and see where data is missing—without presenting illustrations or SI output as NASA measurements.
details:
Flame in Freefall – AI-Powered Space Fire Safety Intelligence

1. What Does Our Project Do?

Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered scientific intelligence platform designed to transform NASA's microgravity combustion research into accessible, meaningful, and actionable fire safety insights.

Fire behaves differently in microgravity compared to Earth. Understanding these differences is essential for protecting astronauts aboard spacecraft, lunar habitats, and future Mars missions.

Our platform brings relevant NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion investigations into one interactive research environment, helping users discover experiments, explore scientific findings, compare experimental conditions, and understand their relevance to space fire safety.

2. How Does It Work?

The platform provides five major capabilities:

NASA Experiment Explorer: Organizes important combustion investigations, including BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, FLEX-2, SAFFIRE, SAME, SAME-R, and ACME. Users can explore experimental objectives, fuels, conditions, available datasets, reports, and publications.

AI Research Copilot: Enables users to ask natural-language questions about microgravity combustion. It helps summarize research, explain scientific concepts, compare investigations, and provide source-linked answers.

Scientific Data Visualization: Presents available experimental parameters through interactive visualizations, including oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, fuel properties, temperature, and combustion behavior.

Experiment Comparison: Helps researchers compare investigations and identify similarities and differences in their experimental conditions and objectives.

Fire Safety Intelligence: Connects scientific research to fire prevention, detection, and suppression requirements for spacecraft, Moon bases, and Mars habitats.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

Our project aims to make decades of NASA combustion research easier to discover, understand, and interpret.

Its potential benefits include:

  • Reducing the time required to find relevant combustion research.
  • Helping researchers compare different microgravity experiments.
  • Making complex scientific findings easier to understand.
  • Supporting research into material flammability and fire suppression.
  • Identifying investigations relevant to future space habitats.
  • Highlighting potential applications of space fire safety research on Earth.

Our long-term vision is to support safer human space exploration through better access to scientific evidence and research intelligence.

4. Technology and Tools Used

The project was developed using modern web technologies and AI-assisted development tools.

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.
  • Animations: GSAP and ScrollTrigger.
  • Data Visualization: Recharts.
  • Artificial Intelligence: Google Gemini API, if integrated.
  • Development Assistance: Google AI Studio and ChatGPT.
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The key innovation is connecting NASA's historically distributed combustion research into a unified, AI-assisted scientific intelligence experience.

Rather than simply displaying scientific documents, Flame in Freefall aims to connect investigations through intelligent search, research summaries, comparative analysis, visualizations, and mission-oriented insights.

The platform focuses on translating complex combustion science into information that is more accessible to researchers, students, and aerospace engineers.

6. Factors Considered

During development, we considered:

  • The unique behavior of flames in microgravity.
  • The importance of oxygen concentration and atmospheric pressure.
  • Differences between solid, liquid, and gaseous fuel experiments.
  • The importance of airflow and environmental conditions.
  • Fire prevention, detection, and suppression requirements.
  • The safety needs of spacecraft, lunar habitats, and Mars missions.
  • Scientific accuracy, source reliability, and transparency of AI-generated interpretations.

Our Vision

"Better Science. Smarter Safety. A Safer Future Beyond Earth."

Flame in Freefall aims to bridge the gap between NASA's microgravity combustion research and the next generation of intelligent space fire safety solutions.
